summary: KS3 experimental probability treats relative frequency (frequency ÷ number of trials) as an ESTIMATE of an underlying probability — and the only available route when a device is biased or its structure unknown (a drawing pin, a bent coin, a weighted die, a real-world event), because its probability cannot be obtained from symmetry. Learners record outcomes in a frequency table, compute relative frequencies, compare with theoretical values where they exist, and reason that the estimate becomes more reliable as trials increase. The central insight: for a device with no symmetry-derived value, the settled relative frequency IS the best estimate, and that reliability is earned by running many trials rather than by trusting a short run.
misconceptions: Reporting the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one, even for a biased/unknown device that has no calculable value
Concluding a device is biased (or fair) from too few trials (law of small numbers)
Thinking absolute counts must even out exactly with more trials (the 'due' fallacy) rather than relative frequency converging
Treating a small-sample relative frequency as a reliable estimate of the true probability

activities.title: Drop a drawing pin and watch the estimate settle
steps: Take a drawing pin (or a visibly bent coin) whose true point-up probability cannot be worked out from symmetry, and a frequency table with a relative-frequency (f ÷ n) column.
Drop the pin 50 times, recording point-up/point-down tallies, then compute relative frequency = point-up frequency ÷ 50.
State this relative frequency as your best estimate of the probability, and note explicitly that there is no theoretical value to calculate from symmetry because the pin is not symmetric.

Reach a much larger number of trials and recompute the relative frequency: pool the whole class's physical drops (same type of pin, dropped the same way onto the same kind of surface) to get into the hundreds, and/or use a hidden-true-probability pin/coin simulator (with the same frequency table and relative-frequency line) to reach 500 then 5000 trials quickly. Note that the simulator's settled value estimates the simulator's hidden probability, not your own pin's. Watch how the value jumps around early and then tends to settle near a steady figure.
Decide how much you would trust the 50-drop figure versus the large-trials figure, and say why.

Use your best estimate for your pin (from your own or pooled class drops of the same kind of pin) × number of trials to predict roughly how many point-ups to expect in a fresh run of, say, 200 drops, recognising that the actual count will vary around that prediction.
activities.insight: When a device is biased or its structure is unknown there is no formula to reach for — you must run trials. The relative frequency you read off IS your best estimate of a probability you could not calculate from symmetry, and that estimate earns its reliability from the number of trials: a 50-drop figure is rough and jumpy, while a settled line after many hundreds or thousands of trials is much more reliable, though still an estimate.

activities.title: Fair-device check: experimental versus theoretical on one scale
steps: Toss an ordinary coin (or roll a fair die), record outcomes in a frequency table, and compute the relative frequency for each outcome.
Mark both your experimental relative frequency and the theoretical probability on the same 0-to-1 scale.
Explain a small gap between them as expected short-run variation rather than a mistake or evidence that the coin is biased.
Repeat with more tosses (or pool data) and see whether the experimental value tends to settle closer to the theoretical one.
activities.insight: Where a theoretical value does exist, relative frequency can be compared with it: discrepancies in a short run are normal variation, and the experimental value tends toward the theoretical as trials increase. This frames why, for a biased device with no symmetry-derived value, the relative frequency is all you have.

activities.title: Compute and judge reliability from given tables
steps: Given a completed frequency table, fill in the relative-frequency column (each outcome's frequency ÷ total trials).
Decide, for a bent coin, which of two samples (e.g. 30 trials versus 800 trials) gives the more reliable estimate of its bias, and justify your choice.
Explain in a sentence why you cannot calculate the bent coin's probability from symmetry.
activities.insight: Computing relative frequency from a table and judging sample-size reliability are skills that can be practised and checked — but they sit on top of the run-and-stabilise experience, which is where the meaning of 'more trials → better estimate' actually comes from.

checkQuestion: Give the child a drawing pin (or a visibly bent coin) and a frequency table. Say: 'Find the probability that this pin lands point-up. Drop it 50 times, record the results, and tell me your best estimate of the probability — and whether 50 drops is enough.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they compute relative frequency from their data or try to state a theoretical 1/2, how they treat the variation, and whether they judge 50 drops as limited.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: records point-up/point-down in the table, computes relative frequency = point-up frequency ÷ 50, and offers THAT as the best estimate — recognising there is no theoretical value to calculate because the pin is not symmetric — while noting that 50 drops gives only a rough estimate and more trials would make it more reliable.
